memory_candidates.content: When one commit site in a dispatch pipeline must land only SOME hunks of a shared file that also carries another task's foreign uncommitted hunk, the mechanized git-commit-phase.sh/git-commit-scoped.sh wrappers are unsafe for that one file: both call `git add` on their given pathspec, which stages the file's FULL current working-tree diff, foreign hunk included. A safe technique: isolate the task's own hunks into a sub-patch (`git diff` then hand-trim to the relevant @@ hunks), `git apply --cached` it, temporarily swap the working tree to match the now-staged content (so a wrapper's own `git add` becomes a no-op), commit, then restore the working tree to its prior (foreign-hunk-included) state. CAVEAT proven the hard way: this workaround does NOT survive a LATER commit at the same file (e.g. a phase-close commit) if that later commit's own pathspec includes the same file — its `git add` re-stages the full working-tree diff including the restored foreign hunk, silently misattributing it. The only durable fix is to never let a later mechanized commit's pathspec include a file with a known-foreign pending hunk, or to resolve/rebase the foreign hunk out of the working tree entirely before the next commit touching that file.

A bash test suite that needs to pass per-case dynamic environment variables into a call to one of its OWN shell functions must never prefix that call with the external `env` command (`env VAR=val my_function` fails: env execs a binary named 'my_function', which does not exist). Use bash's native simple-command prefix-assignment instead (`VAR=val my_function ...`), which works for functions exactly as for external commands. For an array of VAR=val strings collected dynamically, prefix-assignment via array expansion does NOT work (`"${ARR[@]}" my_function` fails identically, since bash's assignment-prefix detection is a parse-time check on literal tokens, not a post-expansion one) -- instead `export "${ARR[@]}"` (export DOES accept multiple NAME=value arguments) inside the same command-substitution subshell (or an explicit `( ... )` subshell) scopes the exports to just that one call without leaking them to later test cases.

Writing a bash test case for a script's 'no credential resolvable' / failure path MUST isolate HOME to a directory with no real credential file (and ideally also unset the relevant TOKEN/HOST env vars) even when the test's intent is 'no token is set' -- otherwise the script under test silently falls back to the REAL machine's own credential file (e.g. ~/.sapience/config.json) and makes a genuine, unintended live call against the real external service. A test that merely omits setting the credential env var is NOT sufficient isolation if the script's own resolution precedence falls through to a real config file on disk.

sapience_notes.subject: Sapience /v1/people/projects/share response shape
sapience_notes.value: When sharing a project with `to: [person_id]`, the server's success response is `{ok: true, project: {kind, key, name}, to: [names], share: {...register-row fields including id}}`. The channel's actual server-minted cid lives at `.share.id`, NOT `.project.key` or `.project.cid` -- `.project.key` is only the slug the caller itself sent in the request body, echoed back unchanged. Confirmed by tracing brain_server.py's _people_project_share -> people_share_project -> project_public -> people_public chain, where people_public sets `id: ch.get('id', '')`.

sapience_notes.subject: Sapience GET /v1/people response shape
sapience_notes.value: GET /v1/people returns {ok, people: [{id, name, channels, since, shares, chats, projects}], count, me, me_id}. `me_id` is this brain's own seat id (via _ch_seat(tok)); `people[].id` is each connection's seat id. Neither value should ever be hardcoded by a client script -- both must be discovered at runtime via this one call.

sapience_notes.subject: REPO_LINK_FOR dark-path project binding
sapience_notes.value: The purpose-built repo-link server-side mechanism (project_cid on every call, project_room_contribute writing straight into the room) is gated by the REPO_LINK_FOR env var on the server and is OFF for this token/deployment as of 2026-11-19: a bogus project_cid probe against /ask returned a normal answer with no project_rejected key, and the installed ~/.sapience/mcp.py client has zero occurrences of project_cid. The decision made here was to adopt repo_link.py's exact .sapience/project.json file format anyway (committed JSON, read back today by this repo's own scripts) so the identical file becomes natively supported the moment the flag is enabled, without any migration.

sapience_notes.subject: Sapience project ownership and note-flow mechanics
sapience_notes.value: Creating (vs. merely joining) a Sapience project matters mechanically, not just as a preference: the server's project_split_confirmed computes cross = doors & (sent | added | first_doors-if-owner-and-not-sent). A non-creator member with auto:false gets an empty intersection, so a tagged note lands as a suggestion only its author sees. The creator/owner, with follow:true, gets notes flowing without a per-note confirm. This is why a dedicated repo-binding task creates a FRESH project rather than reusing an existing received one.
